answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1856–1915 · educator, author & founder of Tuskegee Institute
answer.sourceLine: Genuinely his. The line appears verbatim — opening “I have learned that…” — in Chapter II (“Boyhood Days”) of his 1901 autobiography Up From Slavery, and the same passage was printed a year earlier in his serialized memoir in The Outlook (10 November 1900).

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: 1901 (Doubleday, Page & Co.); passage first ran in The Outlook, 10 Nov 1900

source.excerpt: I used to picture the way that I would act under such circumstances; how I would begin at the bottom and keep rising until I reached the highest round of success. In later years, I confess that I do not envy the white boy as I once did. I have learned that success is to be measured not so much by the position that one has reached in life as by the obstacles which he has overcome while trying to succeed.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ traces the earliest printing to Washington’s memoir installment in The Outlook, 10 November 1900.
The line appears verbatim in Chapter II of Up From Slavery (1901) ↗, opening “I have learned that…”
The same thought reappears in a 1915 account of Washington’s speech at a Harriet Tubman tribute, per Quote Investigator ↗.
source.excerptNote: From Chapter II of Up From Slavery, reflecting on his childhood envy of white boys who seemed to face no obstacles.

author.name: Booker T. Washington
author.heading: About Booker T. Washington
author.metaLine: 1856–1915 · American educator, author & founder of Tuskegee Institute
author.bio: Booker Taliaferro Washington was born into slavery in Virginia and rose to become the most prominent Black educator and public figure in the United States at the turn of the twentieth century. In 1881 he founded the Tuskegee Normal and Industrial Institute in Alabama. His 1901 autobiography Up From Slavery — the source of this line — became one of the most widely read American memoirs of its era.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: Booker T. Washington’s name is one of the internet’s biggest magnets for fabricated inspirational lines — but this one is the real thing. The main pitfall is misquotation, not misattribution.

items.why: Many versions drop “while trying to succeed” or the opening “I have learned that,” and some swap “he has overcome” for “one has overcome.” The full, exact sentence is in Chapter II of Up From Slavery ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The attribution is genuine: the line is verbatim Booker T. Washington, first printed in The Outlook in 1900 and collected in Up From Slavery in 1901, as documented by Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Washington wrote this reflecting on his boyhood, when he envied white children who seemed to inherit success without struggle. Having been born into slavery and worked his way up through manual labor and self-education, he reframed success itself: what counts is not the height you reach but the distance you climbed to get there.
The line became one of the most quoted passages in Up From Slavery, a memoir that shaped American ideas about self-improvement and Black advancement at the turn of the twentieth century.
